title: Just the edge of his cloak

card.keepWhy: Faith you can hold, reaching for him.

sources: Mark 5:25-34 (a woman ill for twelve years, who had spent all she had on physicians and grew worse; she comes behind him in the crowd: “If I shall touch but his garment, I shall be whole”; she is healed at once; Jesus, knowing power had gone out from him, turns: “Who hath touched my garments?”; the disciples point to the thronging crowd; she comes fearing and trembling, falls down and tells him all the truth; “Daughter, thy faith hath made thee whole: go in peace”). Parallels: Matthew 9:20-22, Luke 8:43-48 (the hem or fringe of his garment).
Catechism of the Catholic Church 1667-1679 (sacramentals: sacred signs instituted by the Church that prepare people to receive grace; not magic; popular piety), 1113 and 1210 (the seven sacraments).
Palm Sunday palms kept at home, holy water as a reminder of baptism, saints’ medals: common Catholic sacramentals.
Comparative note: Orthodox Christians keep icons and blessed objects at home; many Protestant traditions use few or no blessed objects.
check: The woman’s illness is left unnamed (“ill for twelve years”) for a gentle telling; Mark describes a flow of blood. Confirm this is acceptable.
Comparative line on Orthodox and Protestant practice is simplified; confirm.

hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? is there one object from your family’s faith that you still keep, or still remember?
options: then keep it close while you listen. this story is about holding on.
hold that picture in mind. you’ll see why it matters.
that’s okay. this story is about reaching out with what you’ve got.

steps.line: A crowd pressed around Jesus on a narrow street. In it was a woman who had been ill for twelve years. She had spent everything on doctors, and only got worse.

steps.q: Twelve years of bleeding made her “unclean” under the law, and anyone she touched too. She means to reach Jesus. How does she go about it?
o: Comes up behind him in the crowd
Asks his friends to bring her to him
Waits for him at the door of a house
steps.why: Mark 5:27: she came up behind him in the crowd. Under Leviticus her touch passed on uncleanness, so slipping close to a teacher unseen was bold.

steps.line: She thought: if I can just touch his clothes, I’ll be well. She reached through the crowd, touched the edge of his cloak, and she was healed.
Jesus stopped. “Who touched my clothes?” His friends said: look at this crowd, everyone is touching you.

steps.q: He keeps looking around. What does the woman do?
o: Slips away, healed, before he finds her
Comes forward, trembling, and tells all
Stays hidden and thanks God quietly
steps.why: She could have slipped away healed. Instead she comes forward and tells the whole truth.

steps.line: Trembling, she came forward, knelt at his feet, and told him the whole truth.
He said, “Daughter, your faith has made you well. Go in peace.”

steps.q: She was already healed. Why does Jesus make her come forward at all?
o: To scold her for touching him unasked
So everyone hears she’s healed, and welcome
To know who to give the credit to
steps.why: Many readers see it this way: the healing was private, but twelve years of being shut out were public. Now the crowd hears him call her “daughter.”

steps.q: Matthew and Luke say she touched the fringe of his cloak. Jewish men wore tassels there, as the Torah commands. What were they for?
o: To show a man was a rabbi
To keep the cloak from fraying
steps.why: Numbers 15: tassels, tzitzit, so you see them and remember the commandments. She reached for the part of his clothes that pointed to God.

steps.line: Today, many Catholic homes keep small holy things: a saint’s medal, a palm behind the crucifix, holy water, a candle by a grandmother’s photo.
steps.label: today

steps.q: Match each thing to what it’s for.
pairs: asking a friend in heaven to pray
steps.why: An abuela’s altarcito, a Santo Niño in a Filipino living room, an Irish grandmother’s holy water by the door. Different shapes, one faith.

say: the church has one word for these things: sacramentals. small blessed objects and gestures, like holy water, ashes or a rosary. not magic, not lucky charms: reminders that point you to God, the way her hand reached for him.

the seven big moments, like baptism and the eucharist, are the sacraments. sacramentals are the small signs around them. orthodox homes keep their icons; many protestants keep few of these things. whatever your family kept, it was a way in.

steps.q: The seven big rites are sacraments. Holy water and medals are sacramentals. What’s the difference?
o: Sacraments come from Christ; sacramentals from the Church
Sacramentals are older and more local
Sacraments are for church; sacramentals for home
steps.why: The Catechism says Christ gave the sacraments; the Church adds sacramentals, which prepare hearts for grace. Like her hand on the cloak, they point past themselves.

today.say: find one thing your family kept: a medal, a photo, a rosary in a drawer. hold it for a moment today, and let it remind you of who it belonged to, and who they prayed to.
options: hold it gently. that’s faith you can hold.
that counts. sometimes the reaching is the prayer.
